assumptions: Target customers operate enough changing third-party AI systems to need evidence review more often than an annual audit.
Vendor and public sources can be monitored and used lawfully at commercially viable cost.
Customers will accept evidence packets as workflow inputs rather than require advisers to recreate the work.
Human review can be restricted to ambiguous material changes without destroying subscription margins.
evidence_needed_for_higher_score: Paid design-partner contracts showing system counts, observed change frequency, accepted packet rate, analyst hours avoided, false-alert rate, legal source rights, renewal intent, and channel acquisition economics.

factors.name: Core insight
factors.rationale: Treating post-approval vendor and model changes as controlled evidence deltas is a specific and credible insight that addresses a gap left by one-time AI assessments.

factors.name: Customer pain and willingness to pay
factors.rationale: Documentation and monitoring duties support recurring work, but the packet does not quantify audit rework, missed-change losses, system counts, or any buyer commitment to this product.

factors.name: Business model and economics
factors.rationale: Per-system subscription revenue could recur and scale, yet pricing, acquisition payback, source licensing, expert review, integration, liability, and channel-share costs are all still assumptions.

factors.name: Market and beachhead
factors.rationale: Regulated and high-consequence AI users are a meaningful market, but the proposed beachhead spans several sectors and lacks evidence of a dense segment with enough third-party systems and a named recurring-control owner.

factors.name: Competitive position and domination potential
factors.rationale: Vendor neutrality and cross-framework mapping are useful, but GRC suites, model-governance platforms, advisers, hyperscalers, and model vendors can bundle much of the workflow.

factors.name: Expansion potential
factors.rationale: A proven delta engine could expand across vendors, AI use cases, control frameworks, sectors, and EU jurisdictions without changing its basic recurring evidence unit.

factors.name: Defensibility and durability
factors.rationale: Reviewer outcomes and false-alert history could improve relevance, but the company owns no source feed, channel position, or exclusive workflow and relies on externally controlled evidence.

factors.name: Strength of advantage
factors.rationale: The founder's AI and analytical fit helps product execution, but there is no demonstrated regulatory authority, proprietary dataset, customer access, or partner commitment.

factors.name: Timing and momentum
factors.rationale: AI Act implementation, rapidly changing model estates, and maturing governance ownership create a strong near-term reason to establish continuous rather than annual evidence control.

factors.name: Distribution
factors.rationale: Audit, GRC, cyber, privacy, and legal channels are logical, but none is signed and partner-led enterprise adoption still entails trust, security review, and unclear customer ownership.

factors.name: Execution and risks
factors.rationale: A bounded prototype is feasible, but lawful source access, alert precision, expert escalation, security review, false assurance, and the legal-advice boundary compound execution risk.

highest_value_structural_change: Secure a multi-year workflow and distribution agreement in one narrow regulated vertical, with customer-authorized vendor evidence access and payment tied to accepted material-change packets rather than generic monitoring.
main_structural_strength: The product turns a recurring external change into a repeatable, source-provenanced control event that can become embedded in an existing governance workflow.
primary_score_limiter: No recurring distribution right, customer workflow position, vendor feed, or quantified willingness to pay is controlled or evidenced.
strongest_disconfirming_evidence: Customers may handle changes inside existing GRC, procurement, and annual-audit processes while model vendors and hyperscalers increasingly publish their own structured compliance portals.
